output.title: Design against untested assumptions by narrowing the decision
output.body:
If you are deciding whether to automate a recurring workflow, the real risk is not the tool. It is the assumption that a demo proves the live job will behave the same way.

For a small business owner, I would narrow the decision to one question: is this a repeatable task with a measurable outcome, already living in digital tools and English-language documents, or is it still too messy to hand over? If the answer is unclear, the build is probably premature.

A good test is simple: write down one workflow, how often it happens, where the data comes from, who approves the result, and what must stay human. That last part matters. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

Bareni’s working rule is to work inside the customer’s environment, with finished code handed over and accounts kept in the customer’s name from the start. That is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not a warranty.

So the next step is not “use AI everywhere.” It is to make the assumption visible before you spend time on the build. One page of notes is usually enough to show whether the workflow is ready, or whether manual work still wins. The build stays technical; the decision stays yours.
